blocks.text: Carbohydrates are naturally occurring organic compounds. The word "carbohydrate" literally means "hydrated carbon". Carbohydrates are synthesised as the primary products of photosynthesis: when carbon dioxide is reduced during photosynthesis, the resulting carbohydrate molecule contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the molar ratio 1:2:1. Their empirical formula is C(H2O)n, where n is the number of carbon atoms.
Carbohydrates are also known as saccharides (Latin saccharum, sugar) and are classified into three groups after this name: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides.
1. Monosaccharides

Monosaccharides (simple sugars) are made of a single sugar molecule. They are easily soluble in water and may have 3 to 7 carbon atoms; they are further classified into subgroups by the number of carbon atoms. Pentoses and hexoses are the most common and are found in all living organisms. Hexoses play the central role in energy storage: the primary energy-storage molecule is glucose, with seven energy-storing C-H bonds, and its empirical formula is C6H12O6 or (CH2O)6.

blocks.text: Isomers of monosaccharides

Molecules that have the same number of atoms (the same molecular formula) but differ in how the atoms are arranged (different structural formula) are isomers of each other. Glucose is not the only monosaccharide with the formula C6H12O6: fructose and galactose have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas. These structural and orientation differences have important consequences in the making of polymers. In fructose the double-bonded oxygen is attached to an internal carbon (number 2) rather than a terminal one, so glucose and fructose are structural isomers. Glucose and galactose differ in the orientation of one hydroxyl (OH) group, at carbon number 4, so glucose and galactose are stereoisomers.

blocks.text: Common five-carbon (pentose) sugars include ribose and deoxyribose, found in nucleic acids and ATP, and ribulose, a precursor in photosynthesis.

blocks.text: Ring structures of monosaccharides

In solution most monosaccharides form ring structures. A ring forms when an oxygen bridge develops between two carbon atoms of the same sugar molecule. In glucose the oxygen bridge develops between carbon 1 and carbon 5, forming a six-cornered ring (pyran). In galactose too the bridge forms between carbons 1 and 5, again a six-cornered pyran ring. In fructose the bridge forms between carbons 2 and 5, giving a five-cornered ring (furan). When ribose goes into solution the bridge develops between carbons 1 and 4, so a five-cornered furan ring forms.

There are two forms of D-glucose, alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-glucose, which differ only in the direction of the OH group on carbon 1: alpha-D-glucose has the OH on the lower side, beta-D-glucose on the upper side. When many alpha-D-glucose molecules join together they form the polymer starch; when many beta-D-glucose molecules join they form the polymer cellulose.

Below: alpha-D-glucose with the carbon 1 OH down and beta-D-glucose with the carbon 1 OH up, highlighted.

blocks.title: Fischer and Haworth projections
blocks.text: These are two ways to represent the structure of sugar molecules. The Fischer projection, devised by the German chemist Emil Fischer in 1891, shows the carbohydrate in its open-chain form. The Haworth projection, named after the British chemist Sir Norman Haworth, shows sugars in their cyclic forms.

blocks.alt: D-glucose (linear form) drawn as a Fischer projection with carbons numbered 1 (CHO) to 6 (CH2OH), with two red arrows to Haworth rings of alpha-D-glucose (carbon 1 OH down) and beta-D-glucose (carbon 1 OH up), each with all H, OH and carbon numbers.
blocks.caption: Fischer and Haworth projections of glucose (side box) (original drawing after the textbook's side box on Fischer and Haworth projections).

blocks.text: 2. Disaccharides

Disaccharides are made from two monosaccharides by dehydration synthesis. The covalent bond between two monosaccharides is a glycosidic bond. On hydrolysis they yield the monosaccharide monomers of which they are made. Compared with monosaccharides they are less soluble in water. The physiologically important disaccharides are maltose, lactose and sucrose.

items: Maltose (malt sugar) is made of two glucose monomers attached by a 1,4-glycosidic bond between carbon 1 of one glucose and carbon 4 of the other. It is found in many cereals (wheat, corn and others) and is also formed, as an intermediate product, during the digestion of starch.

blocks.alt: Two alpha-glucose Haworth rings with carbon numbers; the OH on carbon 1 of the first and the HO on carbon 4 of the second are highlighted. An arrow leads down, releasing H2O, to maltose: the rings joined by an O between carbon 1 and carbon 4, labelled 1,4-glycosidic linkage.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.15: Dehydration synthesis of one maltose by the condensation of two glucose (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.15).

items: Lactose (milk sugar) is made of one glucose and one galactose subunit: galactose 1-4 glucose. It is found only in mammalian milk and is the main source of energy for infant mammals.

blocks.alt: Two Haworth rings with carbon numbers: a galactose subunit (carbon 4 OH up) whose carbon 1 is joined through an O to carbon 4 of a glucose subunit. Labels: Galactose subunit, Glucose subunit, 1,4-glycosidic linkage.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.16: Structure of lactose (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.16).

items: Sucrose (cane sugar) is made of one glucose and one fructose subunit: glucose 1-2 fructose. It is the most familiar disaccharide, also known as table sugar, and acts as a sweetener in our food. It is also found in the phloem vessels of higher plants, where it is the transport product for conducting glucose to and from different parts of the plant; that is why it is also called the transport disaccharide.

blocks.alt: A glucose ring (six-membered, carbon numbers 1 to 6) whose carbon 1 is joined through an O to carbon 2 of a fructose ring (five-membered, carbon numbers 1 to 6, HOCH2 at carbon 1). Labels: Glucose subunit, Fructose subunit, 1,2-glycosidic linkage.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.17: Structure of sucrose (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.17).

blocks.title: High-fructose corn syrup
blocks.text: By 1950 food sweeteners were taken from sucrose extracted from sugarcane and beet; a small part of the market obtained sweeteners by breaking the starch of corn into glucose, but glucose is only half as sweet as sucrose, so this was no serious rival. In the 1980s a method was developed to convert the glucose from corn starch into its isomer fructose, which is even sweeter than sucrose. The resulting high-fructose corn syrup is inexpensive and has replaced sucrose in many prepared foods; the manufacturers of cola soft drinks, once the largest commercial users of sucrose in the world, have almost completely replaced it with high-fructose corn syrup.
3. Polysaccharides

Polysaccharides are the most complex and most abundant carbohydrates in nature. They are long chains of many monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds. The three important polysaccharides are starch, glycogen and cellulose.
Starch

Starch is the plant storage polysaccharide. It is insoluble and forms starch granules inside many plant cells; because it is insoluble it does not change the water potential of plant cells, so it does not cause the cells to take up water by osmosis. Starch is not a pure substance but a mixture of amylose and amylopectin. Amylose is a chain of glucose monomers with 1,4-glycosidic linkages; it is straight and unbranched but tends to coil into a helix. Amylopectin is also a chain of glucose monomers with 1,4-glycosidic linkages, but it also has branches with 1,6-glycosidic linkages, so it has more ends that can be broken more quickly by amylase enzymes. Both amylose and amylopectin are broken down by the enzyme amylase into maltose, though at different rates.

blocks.alt: (a) Amylose: a single unbranched chain of glucose beads coiled into a helix, seen from the side as loops. (b) Amylopectin: a chain of glucose beads with side branches.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.18: (a) amylose, (b) amylopectin (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.18).

blocks.text: Glycogen

Glycogen is similar in structure to amylopectin: a chain of glucose monomers with 1,4-glycosidic linkages and branches with 1,6-glycosidic linkages. It is made by animals as their storage polysaccharide and is found mainly in muscles and liver. Because it is so highly branched, it can be broken down to glucose very quickly.

blocks.alt: A chain of glucose beads with many branches, some of which branch again: a highly branched molecule.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.19: Glycogen (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.19).

blocks.text: Cellulose

Cellulose is found only in plants, where it is the main component of cell walls. It is a chain of glucose monomers with 1,4-glycosidic linkages, but with a different isomer of glucose. Starch and glycogen contain alpha-glucose, in which the OH group on carbon 1 sticks down from the ring, while cellulose contains beta-glucose, in which the OH group on carbon 1 sticks up. This means that in cellulose alternate glucose molecules are inverted.

blocks.alt: Two rows of four glucose rings with carbon numbers 1 to 6. Starch: all rings the same way up, joined C1-O-C4; arrows to the O bridges labelled Alpha 1-4 glycosidic bonds in starch. Cellulose: every second ring inverted (carbon 6 below), joined C1-O-C4; arrows labelled Beta 1-4 glycosidic bonds in cellulose.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.20: Difference between starch and cellulose (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.20).

blocks.text: This apparently tiny difference makes a huge difference in structure and properties: the alpha 1-4 glucose polymer in starch coils up to form granules, whereas the beta 1-4 glucose polymer in cellulose forms straight chains. Hundreds of these chains are linked together by hydrogen bonds to form cellulose microfibrils, and these make cellulose fibrils. They are very strong and rigid and give strength to plant cells, and so to young plants and to materials such as paper and cotton.

blocks.alt: A plant cell with its cell wall; a magnified piece of the wall shows crossing fibres; one cellulose fibril is drawn as a cylinder whose cut end shows microfibrils; below, parallel cellulose chains of linked glucose rings joined by dashed hydrogen bonds. Labels: Plant cell, Cell wall, Cellulose fibril, Microfibril, Cellulose chains.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.21: Cellulose fibrils in plant cell wall (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.21).

blocks.title: Digesting cellulose
blocks.text: The beta-glycosidic bond cannot be broken by amylase; it needs a specific cellulase enzyme. Some bacteria and some protozoans are the only organisms that possess cellulase. Herbivores such as cows and termites, whose diet is mainly cellulose, have mutualistic bacteria in their guts that digest their cellulose. Humans cannot digest cellulose, and it is referred to as dietary fibre.
Chitin

Chitin is a modified form of cellulose, found in the exoskeletons of crabs, lobsters and insects; it also makes the cell wall of fungi. Like cellulose it is a polymer of glucose, and the linkage between the glucose monomers is like that in cellulose, but in chitin each glucose molecule has been modified by the addition of a nitrogen-containing group. Only a few organisms can digest it.

blocks.alt: Four glucose rings joined by O bridges, alternate rings inverted as in cellulose; on carbon 2 of each ring a circled nitrogen-containing group NH-C(=O)-CH3. Labels: Glucose, Nitrogen-containing group.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.22: A part of the chitin molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.22).

blocks.title: Other polysaccharides
blocks.text: Pectin and lignin are also polysaccharides used as building material; they are present in the cell walls of plant cells. Agar is found in the cell walls of red algae; it is used as a thickener in foods and as the medium on which bacteria and fungi are grown in laboratories. Murein is a sugar-peptide polymer found in the cell walls of prokaryotes.
